description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of the Baal Cycle. Contains composition-specific entries that are not (yet) appropriate for promotion to the central production glossary. Entries here may be promoted to central via the standard overlay→central promotion pattern when they appear in subsequent compositions and acquire cross-corpus reach. Note: the `word-of-tree-whisper-of-stone-mystery-revelation-formula-baal-cycle` overlay entry was promoted to central at the chapter-2 Editor pass (now lives in central glossary as `word-of-tree-whisper-of-stone-mystery-revelation-formula-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible`); chapter-1.json glossaryRefs have been back-edited to point to the new central ID.

entries.lemma: ʾiwrkl — uncertain reading; possibly proper-name or epithet
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic uncertain item: ʾiwrkl at KTU 1.2-iii:6, fragmentary context; no fixed reading in named scholarship
entries.standardEnglish: ʾIwrkl (transliteration retained; Smith 1994 vol 1 leaves untranslated; older editions sometimes proposed 'O Lord(?)' or treated as a deity)
entries.wohChoice: ʾIwrkl(?) (transliteration with parenthetical query, preserving the editorial uncertainty)
entries.rationale: The form *ʾiwrkl* at KTU 1.2-iii:6 has no fixed reading in named scholarship. Smith 1994 vol 1 leaves it untranslated. Older editions occasionally proposed a vocative 'O Lord(?)' or treated *ʾiwrkl* as a deity-name (no further attestation supports this). The fragmentary context (the surrounding lines are heavily lacunar) prevents fixing the reading. The Editor preserves the transliteration with parenthetical query in the surface translation; the line is flagged in the verification-pending list.

entries.lemma: ʾaṣṭ — uncertain (Smith 1994 vol 1: 'striking-weapon'); mʿsṣṣt — uncertain (Smith 1994 vol 1: 'smiting-weapon')
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic uncertain items: ʾaṣṭ and mʿsṣṣt at KTU 1.2-i:44, in the scene where Baʿlu seizes weapons in his rage at Yammu's messengers; both items obscure
entries.literal: ʾaṣṭ — a striking-(weapon) of some kind; mʿsṣṣt — a smiting-(weapon) of some kind
entries.standardEnglish: striking-(weapon) / smiting-(weapon) (Smith 1994 vol 1 — tentative readings); Pardee 2003 leaves the line largely untranslated
entries.wohChoice: striking-(weapon) and smiting-(weapon) (descriptive renderings with parenthetical-marking of the weapon-noun, preserving the editorial uncertainty)
entries.rationale: Both *ʾaṣṭ* and *mʿsṣṣt* at KTU 1.2-i:44 are obscure. Smith 1994 vol 1 reads them as 'striking-weapon' and 'smiting-weapon' respectively, acknowledging that both are obscure. Pardee 2003 leaves the line largely untranslated. The Editor's surface rendering keeps the descriptive 'striking-(weapon)' and 'smiting-(weapon)' formulation with parenthetical-marking; the line is flagged in the verification-pending list. Note that these weapons are distinct from the **named** weapons Yagrush and Ayamur that Kothar later forges and names (KTU 1.2-iv:10-31; covered at central entry `yagrush-ayamur-speech-act-named-divine-weapons-cross-corpus`).

entries.lemma: ḥrn (Ugaritic); possible cognate to the divine name attested at the Hebrew Bible place-name Beth-Ḥôrôn; proto-Semitic *√ḥrn — etymology contested
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic minor divinity invoked in curse-formulae: Ḥôrânu (ḥrn), at KTU 1.2-iii:7 in the curse-invocation against Baʿlu; cross-corpus weak to Hebrew Bible (only the place-name Beth-Ḥôrôn carries the divine name)
entries.standardEnglish: Ḥôrânu (deity, Smith 1994 vol 1); 'a scorching curse' (Gibson 1978 — alternative reading)
entries.wohChoice: Ḥôrânu(?) (parenthetical-query preserves the lexical uncertainty; the deity-reading is preferred)
entries.rationale: Ugaritic *ḥrn* at KTU 1.2-iii:7 — *tbʿrn ḥrn rišk* 'may Ḥôrânu(?) burn your head' — is read by **Smith 1994 vol 1** as the divine name Ḥôrânu, a minor Ugaritic divinity associated with curse-formulae and possibly with the underworld. **Gibson 1978** in CML² reads the lexeme differently as 'a scorching curse / noble curse' (non-divine). The Editor follows Smith with the parenthetical-query in surface English. Cross-corpus to the Hebrew Bible is weak — only the place-name Beth-Ḥôrôn (Josh 16:3, 5; 18:13; etc.) carries the divine name as a fossilized toponym; no Hebrew Bible narrative deploys Ḥôrânu as a deity. The cross-corpus reach is therefore overlay-grade rather than central-grade; promotion to central would require additional attestation at future Ugaritic or Phoenician translations.

entries.lemma: mrzḥ (Ugaritic); marzēaḥ (Hebrew); proto-Semitic *√rzḥ; widely-attested ANE ritual-banquet institution
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic ritual-banquet institution: the marzeḥu, a formal ritual-banquet with possible mortuary and patron-deity associations; cross-corpus to Hebrew marzēaḥ at Amos 6:7 (feast-of-the-sprawlers, bêt marzēaḥ) and Jer 16:5 (bêt marzēaḥ, house of mourning-feast); the institution is attested across the Levant and Mesopotamia from the Late Bronze Age through the Hellenistic period
entries.literal: marzeḥu — formal ritual-banquet; the form *b mrzḥ* at 1.1-iv:4 is 'at/in the marzeḥu-feast'
entries.standardEnglish: marzeḥu / marzeaḥ / marzeach-feast (Smith 1994 vol 1; Pardee 2002; McLaughlin 2001)
entries.wohChoice: marzeaḥ-feast (transliterated; the Hebrew-attested Anglicization 'marzeaḥ' is preferred since it preserves the cross-corpus link to the better-known Hebrew Bible attestations)
entries.rationale: The Ugaritic *mrzḥ* (marzeḥu) is one of the most-discussed ANE ritual-banqueting institutions. At KTU 1.1-iv:4 the formula *yṯb b mrzḥ* 'he sits at the marzeḥu' describes ʾIlu's posture at the banquet scene. Other Ugaritic attestations (KTU 1.114 — *ʾil tšlmn* 'ʾIlu drinks himself stupid' marzeḥu-scene; KTU 1.21 administrative text) document the institution more fully. Cross-corpus Hebrew Bible attestations: **Amos 6:7** *l-rosh golim* / *galeh be-rosh golim* + *v-sar mirzach s'ruchim* '(the leaders will go) at the head of the exiled; the *mirzach* of the sprawlers will depart' — the *mirzach* as the formal feast-institution of the elite-leaders; **Jer 16:5** *al tavo veit marzeach* 'do not enter a house of marzeaḥ' — prophetic prohibition of participation in marzeaḥ-banquets. Named scholarship: **D. Pardee**, *Ritual and Cult at Ugarit* (Atlanta 2002); **J. L. McLaughlin**, *The Marzēaḥ in the Prophetic Literature* (VTSup 86, Leiden 2001); **K. van der Toorn**, 'Funerary Rituals and Beatific Afterlife in Ugaritic Texts and in the Bible,' *Bibliotheca Orientalis* 48 (1991) 40-66. The institution likely had mortuary-religious dimensions (especially in the Hebrew prophetic-polemic context); the Ugaritic attestations also show drinking-feast and patron-deity dimensions. The cross-corpus link to Hebrew marzēaḥ is strong; this entry is overlay-grade for now (cross-corpus reach concentrated in Hebrew Bible), with future promotion to central considered if the institution recurs in subsequent NW-Semitic translations.

entries.lemma: hd (Ugaritic; cognate to Akkadian Adad / Iškur, Hebrew Hadad)
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic divine name: Haddu — the personal name of the storm-deity whose cult-title is Baʿlu ('Lord'); cross-corpus to Hebrew Bible Hadad (1 Kgs 11:14, 19, 21, 23; 2 Sam 8 personal-names) and to Akkadian Adad (the major Mesopotamian storm-god)
entries.literal: Haddu — the personal name of the storm-deity called Baʿlu by cult-title
entries.standardEnglish: Haddu / Hadad (Smith 1994 vol 1; Pardee 2003 — uniform consensus on identity)
entries.wohChoice: Haddu (Ugaritic vocalization preserved; the Ugaritic-vs-Akkadian-vs-Hebrew distinction is kept where the source-text is Ugaritic)
entries.rationale: Ugaritic *hd* (Haddu) is the **personal name** of the storm-deity whose cult-title is **Baʿlu** ('Lord'). At KTU 1.1-v:4, 17 Haddu appears in fragmentary narrative-context (*hd tngṯnh* 'Haddu — she meets him'). At KTU 1.4-vi:51 (*yʿdb hd* 'Hadd arranges') and KTU 1.4-vii:38 (*šnʾu hd* 'the haters of Hadd') the personal name surfaces again in the palace-completion and theophany-aftermath scenes. The cult-title vs personal-name distinction is well-documented: Baʿlu is the title-of-respect ('Lord'), Haddu is the personal-name. Cross-corpus links: Akkadian *Adad* (also written *Iškur* in Sumerian logogram) is the major Mesopotamian storm-god, attested widely from the Old Babylonian period through the Neo-Assyrian period; the cult-and-figure-type is closely parallel to Ugaritic Haddu (though Mesopotamian Adad never quite has the cult-prominence Baʿlu/Haddu has in the West-Semitic world). Hebrew Bible attestations: *Hadad* as a personal-name for Edomite kings (1 Kgs 11:14, 19, 21, 23) and in 2 Sam 8 patronymics. The Hadad-personal-name in Hebrew preserves the West-Semitic divine name in fossilized form. The Hadad-Adad-Haddu cluster is overlay-grade in the Baal Cycle context (the personal-name Haddu appears only rarely in the Cycle; Baʿlu/cult-title is much more frequent). Future promotion to central is possible if Haddu recurs prominently in subsequent Ugaritic translations or if cross-corpus reach into Hebrew sharpens. Named-scholarship: D. Schwemer, *Die Wettergottgestalten Mesopotamiens und Nordsyriens im Zeitalter der Keilschriftkulturen* (Wiesbaden 2001) — comprehensive Old Babylonian / Late Bronze Age storm-god treatment; Smith 1994 vol 1; Day 2000.

entries.source: KTU 1.1 col i (entirely destroyed); KTU 1.1 col ii (top of column lost); KTU 1.1 col iii (top of column lost); KTU 1.2 col i (opening lines fragmentary); KTU 1.2 col ii (broken away entirely); KTU 1.2 col iii (top of column lost); KTU 1.2 col iv (top fragmentary); KTU 1.3 col i (opening lines fragmentary); KTU 1.3 col ii (preceded by lost section); KTU 1.3 col iii (top of column lost); KTU 1.3 col iv (opening lines fragmentary); KTU 1.3 col v (top of column lost); KTU 1.3 col vi (top of column lost); KTU 1.4 col i (top fragmentary); KTU 1.4 col ii (top fragmentary); KTU 1.4 col iii (top of column lost); KTU 1.4 col iv (top of column lost); KTU 1.4 col v (opening lines fragmentary); KTU 1.4 col vi (opening lines fragmentary); KTU 1.4 col vii (opening lines fragmentary); KTU 1.4 col viii (opening lines fragmentary)
entries.partOfSpeech: Editorial-apparatus convention: the convention for handling the substantial column-opening and column-entire lacunae across KTU 1.1-1.4 in the Baal Cycle translation — pre-pending each preserved-section with a `preceding_lacuna` editorial-note-paragraph that follows the Smith 1994 vol 1 / Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 / Pardee 2003 reconstructed-narrative-arc, without restoring lost-text in the surface translation itself
entries.standardEnglish: Smith 1994 vol 1 and Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 supply extensive narrative-reconstruction prose for the lost sections; Pardee 2003 is more conservative; older editions (Gibson 1978; Ginsberg 1955) vary
entries.wohChoice: the WoH translation preserves a *preceding_lacuna* prose-note for each preserved-section, summarizing the named-scholarship reconstructed narrative-arc; restorations within a preserved line (e.g. [ḥšk ʿṣk ʿbṣk ʿ]my pʿnk) follow the bracket-convention; no surface English is supplied for entire-column lacunae
entries.rationale: The Baal Cycle KTU 1.1-1.4 has substantial column-level lacunae: KTU 1.1 col i is entirely destroyed; KTU 1.1 cols ii-iii have their tops lost; KTU 1.2 col ii is broken away entirely with cols i, iii, iv fragmentary at the top; KTU 1.3 cols i-vi have opening or top sections fragmentary or lost; KTU 1.4 cols i-viii have similar opening-line gaps. The Editor's convention for handling these substantial lacunae is to **pre-pend each preserved-section with a `preceding_lacuna` editorial-note-paragraph** that summarizes the named-scholarship reconstructed narrative-arc (Smith 1994 vol 1 for KTU 1.1-1.2; Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 for KTU 1.3-1.4; Pardee 2003 as cross-check) **without restoring lost-text in the surface translation itself**. Restorations within preserved lines (e.g. *[ḥšk ʿṣk ʿbṣk ʿ]my pʿnk* — 'hasten, urge, speed to me, your feet —') follow the standard bracket-convention (central entry `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard`, extended at this pass to cover the Ugaritic KTU 1.3-1.4 refIds). The convention preserves the textual-state honestly while giving the reader the named-scholarship narrative-frame to understand the preserved fragments. The convention applies project-wide to all subsequent NW-Semitic translations with substantial column-level lacunae.

entries.partOfSpeech: Editorial-apparatus convention: the verification-pending disclosure convention for the Baal Cycle translation, the project's first Ugaritic-source text — analogous to the same convention established at the Adapa-pass for Akkadian-source

entries.rationale: The Baal Cycle KTU 1.1-1.4 chapters under translation were produced from a best-effort reconstruction of the Ugaritic alphabetic-cuneiform text based on named scholarly editions (Smith 1994 vol 1 for KTU 1.1-1.2; Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 for KTU 1.3-1.4; Pardee 2003; Gibson 1978 CML²; Ginsberg 1955 ANET; KTU³ 2013). Verification of the sign-by-sign transliteration against the modern critical edition (KTU³ Dietrich-Loretz-Sanmartín 2013) is pending. The Editor preserves the verification-pending status unchanged at this pass; the lens-discipline and glossary work operate on the **sense-of-line** (well-attested across editions for the chapter under translation), not on the sign-level reconstruction. The convention is analogous to the verification-pending disclosure convention established at the Adapa-pass for Akkadian-source. Downstream verification-pass against KTU³ is requested.

entries.source: pdry bt ʾar // ṭly bt rb // ʾarṣy bt yʿbdr (Ugaritic alphabetic-cuneiform); recurring at KTU 1.3-i:22-25; KTU 1.3-iv:14-16, 43-45; KTU 1.4-i:8-10; KTU 1.4-iv:14-16; KTU 1.4-vi:16-17; KTU 1.4-vii:23-24
entries.translit: Pidrayu bittu ʾari // Ṭallayu bittu ribbi // ʾArṣayu bittu Yaʿbudaru
entries.lemma: pdry 'Pidrayu' (light/mist deity, *√pdr); ṭly 'Ṭallayu' (dew deity, *√ṭll); ʾarṣy 'ʾArṣayu' (earth/underworld deity, *√ʾrṣ)
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic divine-name triad: the three daughters of Baʿlu — Pidrayu (Light/Mist), Ṭallayu (Dew/Showers), and ʾArṣayu (Earth) — each with a patronymic-form epithet; the standing triad recurs as a fixed Ugaritic-poetic formula throughout KTU 1.3-1.4; the triad does not survive into Hebrew Bible
entries.literal: Pidrayu daughter of light // Ṭallayu daughter of showers // ʾArṣayu daughter of Yaʿbudaru
entries.standardEnglish: Pidrayu daughter of light, Ṭallayu daughter of showers, ʾArṣayu daughter of Yaʿbudaru (Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2; Pardee 2003; Wyatt 2002)
entries.wohChoice: preserve Ugaritic vocalizations Pidrayu / Ṭallayu / ʾArṣayu with their standing epithets 'daughter of light / daughter of showers / daughter of Yaʿbudaru' in surface English; the triad is a fixed Ugaritic-poetic-formulaic unit; no Hebrew Bible cognate cluster exists
entries.rationale: The Ugaritic *pdry bt ʾar // ṭly bt rb // ʾarṣy bt yʿbdr* triad is one of the most-recurring fixed formulas in the Baal Cycle. The three goddesses are explicitly identified as **Baʿlu's daughters**; their cosmic-meteorological domains are encoded in their names: *pdry* (*√pdr*) — 'light, mist, brightness'; *ṭly* (*√ṭll*) — 'dew, showers' (cognate to Hebrew *ṭal* 'dew'); *ʾarṣy* (*√ʾrṣ*) — 'earth' (cognate to Hebrew *ʾereṣ* 'earth'). Each carries a fixed patronymic-form epithet: *bt ʾar* 'daughter of light', *bt rb* 'daughter of showers', *bt yʿbdr* 'daughter of Yaʿbudaru' (the third epithet's etymology is obscure; *Yaʿbudaru* may be a proper-name for a male divine figure or a place-name; Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 leave the lemma's etymology open). The triad is a **fixed formulaic-unit** of Ugaritic poetic-recurring composition; it appears multiple times across KTU 1.3-1.4 in identical or near-identical form. The triad does not survive into the Hebrew Bible. The overlay-grade entry status reflects the composition-specificity: future Ugaritic translations may extend the triad's appearances, but no cross-corpus reach to other corpora is yet attested. Named scholarship: **M. S. Smith and W. T. Pitard**, *The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Volume 2* (VTSup 114, Leiden 2009); **D. Pardee**, *Ritual and Cult at Ugarit* (Atlanta 2002); **N. Wyatt**, *Religious Texts from Ugarit* (Sheffield 2002).

entries.translit: Qadeš ʾaḥdu ṯukba // ʾAmrar k-kabkabi lĕ-pāni
entries.lemma: qdš 'Qadeš' / ʾamrr 'ʾAmrar' — a binomial-form attendant deity (or two distinct attendants); proto-Semitic *√qdš 'holy', *√ʾmr 'speak'
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic minor divinity: Qadeš-wa-ʾAmrar, the binomial-form attendant of ʾAṯirat, who saddles her mount and goes before her like a star; cross-corpus reach minimal (the lemma qdš 'holy' cognate to Hebrew qōdesh / qādôsh is generic; no specific Hebrew Bible attestation of this divine figure)
entries.literal: Qadeš takes the saddle; ʾAmrar (goes) like a star before her
entries.wohChoice: preserve Ugaritic vocalizations Qadeš and ʾAmrar in surface English; the binomial-attendant-of-ʾAṯirat structural-role is glossed in commentary where the name first appears
entries.rationale: The Ugaritic *qdš* + *ʾamrr* binomial appears at KTU 1.4-iv:7-8 as the attendant(s) of ʾAṯirat: *qdš ʾaḥd ṯkb // ʾamrr k-kbkb l-pnm* 'Qadeš takes the saddle; ʾAmrar (goes) like a star before her'. Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 read *qdš-wa-ʾamrr* as either a single binomial-deity (parallel to the divine-craftsman binomial Kothar-wa-Khasis) or as two distinct attendant-divinities; the textual evidence is mixed. The figure is composition-specific to the Baal Cycle and lacks attested cross-corpus reach (the lemma *qdš* 'holy' is generic NW-Semitic; the specific divine-name binomial of Qadeš-wa-ʾAmrar has no Hebrew Bible attestation). The overlay-grade entry status reflects the composition-specificity. Named scholarship: **M. S. Smith and W. T. Pitard**, *The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Volume 2* (VTSup 114, Leiden 2009); **D. Pardee**, *'The Baʿlu Myth (1.86)'* in CoS 1 (Leiden 2003), pp. 241-274.

entries.source: b ʾalp šd rbt kmn (Ugaritic alphabetic-cuneiform); recurring at KTU 1.3-iv:5; KTU 1.3-vi:15; KTU 1.4-v:24; KTU 1.4-viii:17-18
entries.partOfSpeech: Ugaritic formulaic pilgrimage-distance phrase: 'through a thousand acres, ten thousand hectares' — the standing Ugaritic-poetic doubling for cosmic-pilgrimage-distance; deployed when a deity travels across a vast distance to meet another deity or to reach the cosmic-mountain
entries.literal: through a thousand acres, ten thousand hectares — the cosmic-distance pilgrimage marker
entries.standardEnglish: a thousand acres, ten thousand hectares (Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2; Pardee 2003)
entries.wohChoice: preserve the literal numerical-doubling 'a thousand acres, ten thousand hectares' in surface English; the formula's compositional function (cosmic-distance pilgrimage marker) is glossed in commentary where it first appears
entries.rationale: The Ugaritic formula *b ʾalp šd rbt kmn* 'through a thousand acres, ten thousand hectares' is a standing compositional pilgrimage-distance phrase in the Baal Cycle. It appears at KTU 1.3-iv:5 (ʿAnatu's travel to Baʿlu on Ṣapunu); KTU 1.3-vi:15 (the messengers' travel to Kothar at Memphis-Kaphtor); KTU 1.4-v:24 (ʿAnatu's travel to Baʿlu after ʾIlu's grant); KTU 1.4-viii:17-18 (the messengers' travel to Môtu in the underworld). The formula encodes the **vast cosmic-distance** between the abodes of the deities, marking the pilgrimage-scene as a major cosmographic-narrative transition. The Ugaritic numerical-pair *ʾalp* (1000) + *rbt* (10000) follows the standard Northwest-Semitic poetic-doubling pattern (*šbʿ-šmnh* '7-8'; *ʾalp-rbt* '1000-10000'; cf. Hebrew *ʾelef-rĕvāvāh*). The compositional-feature is composition-specific to the Baal Cycle (and possibly to wider Ugaritic narrative-poetic conventions); cross-corpus reach is minimal. The overlay-grade entry status reflects the composition-specificity. Named scholarship: **M. S. Smith and W. T. Pitard**, *The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Volume 2* (VTSup 114, Leiden 2009); **D. Pardee**, *'The Baʿlu Myth (1.86)'* in CoS 1 (Leiden 2003).
